questions.text: A patient with a drug overdose is admitted with a depressed level of consciousness. ABG shows pH 7.26, PaCO₂ 64 mmHg, PaO₂ 70 mmHg. This is best classified as which type of respiratory failure?

answers.text: Type II (hypercapnic) — failure to remove CO₂ from a decreased respiratory drive
Type I (hypoxemic) — a primary oxygenation failure with an elevated A-a gradient
Chronic respiratory failure secondary to COPD
Combined refractory hypoxemia from intrapulmonary shunt

questions.text: Which condition increases alveolar dead space by creating a region with ventilation but no perfusion (V/Q approaching infinity)?

answers.text: Pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary edema
Atelectasis
Pneumonia

questions.text: Newton's equation of motion for the respiratory system is expressed as Pressure = (Raw × Flow) + (Volume / Compliance). What does this equation describe?

answers.text: The pressure required to drive gas into the lungs must overcome both airway resistance and elastic (compliance) forces
The total oxygen delivered equals cardiac output multiplied by arterial oxygen content
Minute ventilation equals respiratory rate multiplied by tidal volume
Dead space ventilation is the difference between arterial and exhaled CO₂

questions.text: Which input power classification describes the most common ICU ventilator?

answers.text: Combination — uses both pneumatic (50 psi gas) and electric power
Pneumatic only — operates from a 50 psi gas source alone, like an IPPB device
Electric only — operates from a wall outlet alone, like most home ventilators
Fluidic only — uses gas logic with no electronic components

questions.text: A ventilator is set to flow triggering. How does the ventilator detect the patient's effort to begin a breath?

answers.text: It senses a drop in the bias (base) flow as the patient draws gas from the circuit
It senses a rise in airway pressure above the baseline (PEEP) level
It waits for the set inspiratory time to elapse before delivering gas
It measures a drop in exhaled tidal volume below the alarm threshold

questions.text: Which set of characteristics correctly describes a spontaneous breath?

answers.text: Patient triggered, baseline targeted, and patient cycled — the patient performs all the work of breathing
Ventilator triggered, volume targeted, and ventilator cycled
Patient triggered, pressure targeted, and flow cycled
Time triggered, time targeted, and time cycled

questions.text: Which of the following is a recognized goal of mechanical ventilation?

answers.text: Reduce the work of breathing and reduce myocardial workload secondary to hypoxemia and increased WOB
Increase intracranial pressure to maintain cerebral perfusion
Maximize FiO₂ to 100% to guarantee adequate oxygen delivery at all times
Eliminate all spontaneous breathing to fully rest the diaphragm permanently

questions.text: Positive pressure ventilation is non-physiologic. Which hazard results from the increased intrathoracic pressure it generates?

answers.text: Decreased venous return, which can reduce cardiac output and urinary output
Increased venous return, which raises cardiac output and urine output
Increased renal perfusion from elevated mean airway pressure
Improved cerebral venous drainage and lowered intracranial pressure

questions.text: Which of the following is a contraindication to initiating mechanical ventilation?

answers.text: A documented DNR/DNI order or medically futile therapy that is contrary to the patient's wishes
PaCO₂ of 58 mmHg with a pH of 7.19
A vital capacity less than 10 mL/kg with a rising respiratory rate
Refractory hypoxemia unresponsive to a non-rebreather mask

questions.text: A patient being considered for NIV is obtunded, cannot protect the airway, and has copious secretions. How should NIV be approached?

answers.text: NIV is contraindicated — inability to protect the airway, excessive secretions, and high aspiration risk are contraindications
Proceed with NIV using a total face mask to overcome the secretion burden
Proceed with NIV but set a high backup rate to compensate for the decreased drive
Proceed with nasal CPAP because it carries no aspiration risk

questions.text: A patient on BiPAP for hypoxemic respiratory failure has an adequate PaCO₂ but persistent hypoxemia (SpO₂ 88%). Which adjustment most directly improves oxygenation?

answers.text: Increase EPAP — it functions like PEEP/CPAP and primarily affects oxygenation/PaO₂
Increase IPAP alone — it primarily affects ventilation/PaCO₂, not oxygenation
Decrease EPAP — lowering baseline pressure recruits more alveoli
Narrow the IPAP–EPAP difference to reduce delivered tidal volume

questions.text: How does the AVAPS mode on a noninvasive ventilator maintain a target tidal volume?

answers.text: IPAP is automatically adjusted between a set minimum and maximum pressure to deliver the targeted Vt
EPAP is automatically increased until the target Vt is reached
A fixed IPAP is set manually and the rate increases to reach the target Vt
The FiO₂ is titrated to maintain the targeted tidal volume

questions.text: In the Spontaneous/Timed (S/T) mode of NIV, what is the purpose of the set respiratory rate?

answers.text: It guarantees a minimum number of breaths per minute if the patient fails to breathe spontaneously
It caps the maximum number of spontaneous breaths the patient may take
It sets the inspiratory time for every spontaneous breath
It determines the rate at which IPAP rises to EPAP

questions.text: Which step is part of the correct initial application of NIV?

answers.text: Elevate the head of the bed above 30°, start with low or zero pressures, and reassess the patient frequently (about every 30 minutes) in the first hours
Lay the patient flat and immediately apply full therapeutic pressures for the best seal
Tightly strap the mask before turning the device on to prevent any air leak
Avoid reassessment for the first several hours to allow the patient to acclimate

questions.text: A patient on NIV develops uncomfortable gastric bloating. What is an appropriate intervention?

answers.text: Administer anti-gas therapy such as simethicone
Increase IPAP to push the trapped gas distally
Switch to nasal pillows to raise delivered pressure
Remove all humidification from the circuit

questions.text: Calculate the predicted IBW and initial tidal volume range (6–8 mL/kg) for a female who is 5'4" (64 inches). IBW(female) = 45.5 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60).

answers.text: IBW ≈ 55 kg; Vt range ≈ 330–440 mL
IBW ≈ 64 kg; Vt range ≈ 384–512 mL
IBW ≈ 55 kg; Vt range ≈ 550–660 mL
IBW ≈ 45 kg; Vt range ≈ 270–360 mL

questions.text: A male patient is 6'0" (72 inches). Using IBW(male) = 50 + 2.3 × (height in inches − 60), what is his predicted IBW and an appropriate initial tidal volume at 8 mL/kg?

answers.text: IBW ≈ 78 kg; initial Vt ≈ 620 mL
IBW ≈ 78 kg; initial Vt ≈ 470 mL is the maximum allowed
IBW ≈ 90 kg; initial Vt ≈ 720 mL
IBW ≈ 72 kg; initial Vt ≈ 430 mL

questions.text: A volume-controlled breath is delivered with a constant inspiratory flow of 60 L/min and an inspiratory time of 0.8 seconds. What tidal volume is delivered? (PIFR × I-time = Vt)

answers.text: 800 mL (1 L/sec × 0.8 sec = 0.8 L)
750 mL

questions.text: A patient is set at a respiratory rate of 12 breaths/min with an I:E ratio of 1:3. What is the inspiratory time? (I-time = cycle time ÷ sum of I:E parts; cycle time = 60 ÷ RR)

answers.text: 1.25 seconds (cycle time 5 sec ÷ 4 = 1.25 sec)
1.67 seconds (5 ÷ 3)
2.0 seconds (6 ÷ 3)
0.75 seconds

questions.text: A patient's set tidal volume is 450 mL and the respiratory rate is 16 breaths/min. What is the minute volume? (Vt × RR = minute volume)

answers.text: 7.2 L/min
4.5 L/min
10.8 L/min
28.1 L/min

questions.text: Anatomic dead space is estimated at approximately 1 mL per pound of ideal body weight. For a patient with an IBW of 160 lb, what is the estimated anatomic dead space?

answers.text: Approximately 160 mL
Approximately 480 mL
Approximately 73 mL
Approximately 30 mL

questions.text: A patient with an IBW of 200 lb is ventilated with a set Vt of 600 mL at a peak pressure of 30 cmH₂O (adult circuit factor 3 mL/cmH₂O) and has 60 mL of alveolar dead space. What is the approximate alveolar tidal volume? (Vt − [anatomic + compressible + alveolar dead space])
A patient with severe obstructive (COPD) physiology is air-trapping. Which I:E ratio adjustment best addresses this?

answers.text: Lengthen expiratory time toward a higher ratio such as 1:4 to 1:6
Use an inverse ratio such as 2:1 to improve oxygenation
Set the ratio to 1:1 to match infant physiology
Shorten expiratory time to a ratio of 1:1.5 to raise mean airway pressure

questions.text: A patient on volume control has the correct tidal volume for IBW, but ABG shows pH 7.28, PaCO₂ 52 mmHg, PaO₂ 96 mmHg. Current RR is 10. Using New RR = (current RR × current PaCO₂) ÷ desired PaCO₂, what rate targets a PaCO₂ of 40 mmHg?

answers.text: RR ≈ 13 breaths/min (10 × 52 / 40 = 13)
RR ≈ 8 breaths/min
Increase tidal volume rather than rate, since the Vt is the problem
RR ≈ 18 breaths/min

questions.text: An ABG shows an isolated oxygenation problem (low PaO₂, normal PaCO₂ and pH). The patient is improving and you are weaning support. What is the correct order for weaning FiO₂ and PEEP?

answers.text: Reduce FiO₂ first to 60%, then begin decreasing PEEP in increments of 2–5 cmH₂O
Decrease PEEP to 0 first, then wean FiO₂ from 100% to 60%
Decrease FiO₂ and PEEP together in equal steps to keep them balanced
Leave FiO₂ at 100% and wean PEEP rapidly to baseline

questions.text: A patient's plateau pressure is 28 cmH₂O on a PEEP of 8 cmH₂O. What is the driving pressure, and is it within the recommended limit?

answers.text: 20 cmH₂O (Pplat − PEEP) — above the recommended limit of < 15 cmH₂O
36 cmH₂O (Pplat + PEEP) — above the limit of < 30 cmH₂O
20 cmH₂O — within the recommended limit of < 30 cmH₂O
8 cmH₂O — within the limit of < 15 cmH₂O

questions.text: A patient is ventilated with a tidal volume of 500 mL, a plateau pressure of 25 cmH₂O, and a PEEP of 5 cmH₂O. What is the static compliance? (Static compliance = Vt ÷ [Pplat − PEEP])

answers.text: 25 mL/cmH₂O — below the normal range of 60–100 mL/cmH₂O
100 mL/cmH₂O — within the normal range
20 mL/cmH₂O — within the normal range
50 mL/cmH₂O — using Vt ÷ Pplat

questions.text: Which change would be expected to INCREASE the peak inspiratory pressure during volume-controlled ventilation?

answers.text: Increased airway resistance (e.g., bronchospasm or secretions)
Increased lung compliance
Decreased tidal volume
Decreased PEEP

questions.text: What is the normal range for mean airway pressure (MAP), and which factor raises it?

answers.text: Normal MAP is about 5–10 cmH₂O; it is raised by increasing PEEP, PIP/tidal volume, I-time, or respiratory rate
Normal MAP is about 20–30 cmH₂O; it is raised only by increasing FiO₂
Normal MAP is about 0–5 cmH₂O; it is raised by decreasing the inspiratory time
Normal MAP is about 30–40 cmH₂O; it is lowered by adding PEEP

questions.text: A low-pressure alarm sounds on a mechanically ventilated patient. What is the most likely cause, and how is the alarm typically set?

answers.text: A leak or circuit disconnection; the alarm is set about 10–15 cmH₂O below the measured PIP
Secretions or bronchospasm; the alarm is set about 10–15 cmH₂O above PIP
Worsening compliance; the alarm is set at twice the measured PIP
Auto-PEEP; the alarm is set equal to the measured plateau pressure

questions.text: What happens when measured airway pressure reaches the high-pressure alarm/limit setting during a breath?

answers.text: Inspiration ends and the ventilator cycles into expiration; the remaining volume or pressure is not delivered
The ventilator delivers a larger breath to overcome the obstruction
The ventilator switches automatically to a pressure-support mode
The alarm is silenced and ventilation continues unchanged

questions.text: Which maneuver is used to directly measure auto-PEEP (intrinsic PEEP) at the bedside?

answers.text: An expiratory hold (expiratory pause) maneuver
An inspiratory hold (inspiratory pause) maneuver
A negative inspiratory force (NIF) maneuver
A vital capacity maneuver

questions.text: During a ventilator check, the monitored total respiratory rate is well above the set mandatory rate and the patient appears under-sedated and in pain. How should the elevated rate be interpreted?

answers.text: A high spontaneous rate from under-sedation, pain, or increased work of breathing
Over-sedation, which characteristically raises the respiratory rate
A normal finding that requires no further assessment
A failed apnea alarm that has stopped backup ventilation

questions.text: Why is a tidal volume alarm set 'close' (with a narrow window) specifically during pressure-control modes?

answers.text: In pressure control the pressure is constant and volume is variable, so delivered Vt changes with compliance and resistance and must be watched closely
In pressure control the tidal volume is fixed, so any deviation signals a circuit fault
Pressure-control modes do not measure exhaled volume, so the alarm substitutes for it
The tidal volume alarm replaces the high-pressure limit in pressure control

questions.text: This pressure–time scalar is recorded during a volume-controlled breath. What abnormality is shown, and how is it corrected?

answers.text: Flow starvation — the set flow is below patient demand (concave/scooped pressure tracing); correct by increasing the PIFR
Auto-PEEP — increase the expiratory time and add a bronchodilator
A circuit leak — check connections and replace the circuit
Decreased compliance — increase PEEP to recruit alveoli

questions.text: This pressure–time scalar is captured with an inspiratory hold. Based on the relationship between PIP and plateau pressure, what does it indicate?

answers.text: Increased airway resistance — a large PIP–Pplat gradient with a normal plateau, seen with secretions, bronchospasm, or a kinked tube
Decreased compliance — PIP and plateau are both elevated and rise together
A circuit leak — the pressure fails to return to baseline
Normal mechanics — the gradient between PIP and plateau is expected to be wide

questions.text: The solid (current) pressure–volume loop is compared with the dashed normal reference loop. What change has occurred and what is the appropriate response?

answers.text: Decreased compliance — the loop has flattened toward the pressure axis (lower slope); increase PEEP and treat the underlying cause
Increased compliance — the loop has become steeper, so reduce PEEP
Increased airway resistance — widen the loop by adding a bronchodilator
A leak — the loop fails to close, so check all connections

questions.text: This volume–time scalar shows the expiratory tracing failing to return to the zero baseline. What does this most likely indicate?

answers.text: A leak in the circuit or around the airway — exhaled volume does not return to baseline
Auto-PEEP — gas is trapped in the alveoli at end-exhalation
Flow starvation — inspiratory flow is below patient demand
Overdistension — the alveoli are being ventilated above safe pressures

questions.text: On this flow–time scalar, the expiratory flow does not return to the zero baseline before each successive inspiration begins. What is shown, and what is an appropriate treatment?

answers.text: Auto-PEEP (air trapping) — treat by decreasing the rate, increasing flow/expiratory time, bronchodilators, or suctioning
Flow starvation — increase the PIFR to meet inspiratory demand
A circuit leak — replace the circuit and recheck connections
Decreased compliance — increase PEEP and tidal volume

questions.text: A patient must be transported 200 miles to a specialized facility. Which mode of inter-hospital transport is indicated by this distance?

answers.text: Airplane (fixed-wing aircraft) — used for distances greater than 150 miles
Ground ambulance — used for distances of 0–80 miles
Helicopter (rotary-wing) — used for distances of 80–150 miles
Ground ambulance — preferred for all distances under 300 miles

questions.text: Which feature is a required capability of a transport ventilator used for a mechanically ventilated patient?

answers.text: Battery backup power, the ability to provide PEEP and FiO₂ up to 1.0, disconnect/low-pressure and high-pressure alarms, and an anti-asphyxia valve
A dual-limb circuit with a heated wick humidifier and built-in capnography
Reliance on wall electrical power only, with no battery requirement
A fixed FiO₂ of 0.21 that cannot be adjusted to conserve oxygen

questions.text: Why is a transport ventilator generally preferred over manual (bag) ventilation during patient transport?

answers.text: It provides more consistent ventilation and avoids the hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis common with manual ventilation
It eliminates the need for a portable oxygen source during the move
It removes the requirement for airway pressure monitoring en route
It guarantees that all gas leaving the cylinder reaches the patient at 100% efficiency

questions.text: Which statement correctly describes the team for transporting a mechanically ventilated patient?

answers.text: At least one member must be proficient in airway management and at least one must be an ACLS provider; a CCATT unit ideally includes a critical care physician, a critical care nurse, and a respiratory therapist
A single respiratory therapist may transport any ventilated patient alone
A physician must personally accompany every transport regardless of stability
Only nursing staff are required; airway and ACLS skills are optional

questions.text: Calculate the rapid shallow breathing index (RSBI) for a patient breathing at 22 breaths/min with a tidal volume of 350 mL, and interpret it. (RSBI = RR ÷ Vt in liters)

answers.text: RSBI ≈ 63 — below 105, a good predictor of weaning success
RSBI ≈ 157 — above 105, predicts weaning failure
RSBI ≈ 7.7 — below 105, predicts weaning success
RSBI ≈ 22 — indeterminate without the minute volume

questions.text: Under what conditions should RSBI data be collected for it to be a valid weaning predictor?

answers.text: After one minute of spontaneous breathing with PEEP 0 cmH₂O and pressure support 0 cmH₂O
During assist/control with full ventilator support and PEEP 5 cmH₂O
After 30 minutes of high-level pressure support (10–12 cmH₂O)
Only while the patient is sedated and apneic on backup ventilation

questions.text: Which ventilatory mechanics value meets the threshold suggesting a patient may be ready for weaning/discontinuation?

answers.text: Vital capacity greater than 15 mL/kg with a respiratory rate of 12–30 breaths/min
Vital capacity less than 5 mL/kg with a respiratory rate of 40 breaths/min
Static compliance less than 25 mL/cmH₂O
An RSBI greater than 105 with a tidal volume of 3 mL/kg

questions.text: Success of weaning depends on four factors. Which of the following is one of them?

answers.text: Psychological factors — anxiety, sleep deprivation, and ICU psychosis can impair weaning
The brand of ventilator used for the spontaneous breathing trial
The time of day the trial is performed
The number of prior intubations the patient has had

questions.text: Regarding weaning timelines, which statement is correct?

answers.text: Most patients wean quickly (within 72 hours), while patients with chronic pulmonary disease or ARDS are more likely to need a prolonged, systematic approach
Most patients require weeks to wean, while only post-op and overdose patients wean within 72 hours
All ventilated patients are weaned on a fixed 7-day protocol regardless of cause
Patients with neuromuscular disease are the easiest and fastest to wean

questions.text: During a ventilator circuit change, at what point in the respiratory cycle should the old circuit be removed and replaced, and what should be ready first?

answers.text: Remove and replace the circuit during exhalation, after a manual resuscitator has been set up and confirmed functional
Remove and replace the circuit during peak inspiration to keep the lungs inflated
Disconnect the circuit without a backup device to minimize the procedure time
Replace the circuit only after extubating the patient to avoid contamination

questions.text: Beyond the routine scheduled interval (commonly every 2 hours), when must an additional patient–ventilator system check be performed?

answers.text: Before obtaining blood gases, following any change in ventilator settings, and after an acute deterioration in the patient's condition
Only once per shift, regardless of changes in settings or patient status
Only when the high-pressure alarm has sounded three or more times
Only immediately before extubation and at no other time
